strait-of-hormuz.summary: Effectively closed to normal commercial traffic since 28 Feb: Iran requires permits and fees through its Strait Authority, a US blockade of Iranian ports has been in force since 14 July, and attacks on ships continue. The IMO recorded 9 tanker attacks in the strait in the week of 28 Sep-5 Oct, the highest weekly total since the war began; a chemical tanker (Acers) was separately struck by projectiles on 7 Oct about 51 nautical miles off Qatar, west of the usual attack cluster, and Iran's IRGC said it struck the LPG tanker NV Sunshine on 9 Oct for taking an unauthorized route (IRGC claim, unverified). Reuters reported, citing officials close to Tehran, that Iran plans to widen threats against ships using routes it hasn't authorized, including Omani-side channels and Gulf of Oman transfer points — a plan that could not be independently verified. President Trump said on 8 Oct the US will not attack Iran before November's midterm elections, that the US blockade remains in force, and that oil is flowing through the strait; he rejected Iran's latest proposal to end the war. Saudi Aramco is in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on the ship-to-ship transfer system that bypasses the strait, and VLCC freight on the Gulf-to-Asia route hit a record near $1.4 million/day as that shuttle system strains vessel supply. Kpler ship-tracking data put Hormuz crude exports at about 8.5 mb/d (roughly 40% below pre-war) in the week to 7 Oct, down from the 13.2 mb/d (about 77% of baseline) Kpler reported for the week to 29 Sep, even as satellite imagery had shown a 'major operational recovery' at Saudi Arabia's Yanbu terminal; Vortexa separately put non-Iranian Gulf oil flows at 81% of pre-war levels in September. Tankers still move mainly under naval escort or shuttle arrangements rather than normal free transit, and many sail with transponders off, so independent counts remain partial; IMF PortWatch's AIS-tracked tanker count for Hormuz averaged just 0.6/day in the week to 11 Oct, down from 1.3/day in late September, though broader tracking shows higher flows since many vessels sail dark. The attack zone widened further on 9 October when the fully laden VLCC GEM NO.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile about 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, outside the strait itself; two more unnamed outbound tankers were then hit by projectiles and caught fire inside the strait on 10 and 11 October, per UKMTO, with crews reported safe in both cases. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on 11 October that the US response to Iran's seven conditions for reopening the strait was ‘insufficient’ and that Tehran would stop responding through the current channel; the US had replied via Qatari intermediaries. Delayed UKMTO and JMIC reports disclosed on 12 Oct showed the 11 Oct toll was larger than first known: six vessels, five tankers and a container ship, were struck that day, the highest single-day total since the war began; one was hit by a drone at Oman's Sohar anchorage and reclassified from 'suspicious activity' to an attack, and JMIC raised its threat assessment for the strait to SEVERE. No group claimed responsibility for any of the six. On 13 October the Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank after a projectile strike (21 crew safe; Iran's unevidenced naval-mine claim was disputed by maritime security firm Marisks), its sister ship GFS Giselle was damaged but reached anchorage, and the bulk carrier Cape Dao — struck 23 September — also went down; the IMO has documented more than 100 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait since the war began. CENTCOM said on 14 October it had destroyed an Iranian-affiliated dhow in the Gulf of Oman on 6 October, alleging it was helping target US Navy ships (CENTCOM claim, unverified). On 15 October CENTCOM said the US and regional partners "control the strait as commercial vessels continue to transit," citing more than 40 commercial transits in the prior 24 hours (CENTCOM claim, unverified); the JMIC advisory for 11-14 October counted about 121 US-facilitated transits, roughly 30 a day and about 22% of the ~138/day pre-war average, and said US forces had redirected 135 commercial vessels and disabled four as of 10-11 October. The IMO put the cumulative toll at 113 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait since the war began as of 14 October; JMIC separately logged 149 confirmed vessel incidents region-wide since 1 March, including eight projectile attacks on four tankers and four containerships on 11 and 13 October and a separate strike near Sohar, Oman, that left two crew of the tanker Petro Dolphin missing. UKMTO's weekly overview (16 Oct) said most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents to it, logged 12 further attacks in its latest period (10 in the strait, one each in the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman), and counted only 254 transits in the week to 14 October (70% below pre-war levels) — of which just 42 were directly AIS-tracked, the rest being unverifiable US-reported 'facilitated' transits. CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on 16 October that about 400 merchant ships transited in the same week and that US forces helped move over 100 million barrels of crude (CENTCOM claim, unverified), a figure UKMTO's own count cannot confirm; Iran's army chief Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami said on 15 October the strait would stay closed until Iran's rights are respected (Iranian claim, unverified). Reuters separately reported, citing tracking group UANI and satellite analysis firm SynMax, that Iran has shipped at least 4.1 million barrels of LPG on eight tankers and one jet-fuel cargo (to Myanmar in September) past the US blockade since mid-July, even as Iran's own crude exports fell to zero in September for the first time since Kpler began tracking the country in 2013. Gulf-to-China VLCC freight rates eased about 8% week on week to 776 Worldscale by 16 October, still near record highs, as Middle East demand cooled and Washington weighed easing shadow-fleet tanker sanctions. UKMTO reported that two tankers were struck 68 and 78 nautical miles northeast of al-Jubail, Saudi Arabia on 16 October, outside the strait itself, which ISW/CTP assessed was likely the work of the IRGC Navy; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately said the ships, each carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, hit naval mines on an unauthorized route (IRGC claim, unverified; no independent confirmation per Reuters). Vitol's Asia head said on 16 October that a shortage of high-sulfur fuel oil for ships will persist even as Hormuz crude flows rise, as Gulf fuel-oil exports fall and refiners favor higher-margin diesel. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on 17 October that two more tankers, each carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, caught fire after hitting naval mines in the strait with their tracking switched off (IRGC claim, unverified; Reuters found no independent confirmation). On 18 October Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran's offer to reopen the strait within seven days of a US acceptance, first made in mid-September, still stands; the US has replied via Qatari mediators, but the two sides remain stuck on Washington's demand that Iran also address its nuclear program. Separately on 18 October, Turkey's energy minister said Ankara will take some of the diesel Russia is supplying under the Trump-Putin deal, after Russia curtailed exports. A tugboat was damaged by two unknown projectiles northeast of Khor Fakkan, UAE on 18 October, injuring one crew member before it continued its route; ISW/CTP assessed Iran likely carried out the strike. On 19 October Bloomberg reported Iran's oil-loading terminals have sat idle since late August, the longest stretch of the war, and that UKMTO logged 25 ships targeted in and around the strait in the first two weeks of October, versus 18 in September and 15 in August; separately, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US will let investors buy and refurbish sanctioned tankers to carry non-sanctioned crude, as Gulf-to-Asia freight rates remain more than six times pre-war levels. On 19 October Yemen's Houthis claimed missile-and-drone strikes on Aramco's Yanbu site, the Shaybah oil field, and airports in Riyadh and Abha; Reuters reported no independent or Saudi confirmation (Houthi claim, unverified). Preliminary Kpler ship-tracking data put combined Middle East oil flows — Hormuz transits plus Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers, Fujairah/Omani terminal loadings and Red Sea exports — at more than 24.5 million bpd in the week to 18 October, edging above the 24.4 million bpd Kpler recorded the week before the war began; Iran's own exports remain excluded and at zero. The IMO's cumulative toll rose to 116 confirmed incidents and at least 24 seafarer deaths in the strait as of 20 October, up from 113 incidents on 14 October. Brent rose to a five-month high near $111/bbl on 20 October amid the renewed Houthi claims. UKMTO's tally for the wider Arabian Peninsula region reached 32 attacks on commercial vessels so far in October as of 21 October, already double September's total of 16, even as most tankers in the area now sail with AIS tracking off; the figure differs from UKMTO's own 25-attack count for the strait area reported on 19 October, a gap likely reflecting different reporting windows rather than a correction. South Korean shipowner Sinokor moved 105.6 million barrels of crude through the strait in September — almost 40% of the month's total and more than the next three owners (Bahri, Kuwait Oil Tanker Company and ADNOC's shipping arm) combined — running short shuttle trips from Gulf terminals to ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman, per ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg (Vortexa, Equasis, Signal Group). The IEA put Gulf-to-Asia tanker freight above $37 a barrel on 21 October, more than five times pre-war levels. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on 22 October that seven commercial vessels, four of them mid ship-to-ship transfer, were struck overnight in the Gulf and the strait; President Trump dismissed the claim on Truth Social as Iran 'making up fake hits, mines, and everything else' to raise oil prices before the 3 November midterms. UKMTO had issued no incident reports matching either account as of this writing, so neither the attack nor the denial is independently established (IRGC claim and Trump statement, both unverified). The New York Times reported, citing US officials, that the US and Israeli militaries are planning a short, intensive operation against Iran for after the midterms; Brent rose to $116.72 on 23 October, its highest close since 29 April, on the reports. JMIC's count for 22-24 October found just 101 transits, about a quarter of the ~138/day pre-war baseline, with about 492 vessels waiting outside the strait as of 25 October, and said the backlog is likely to persist; UKMTO separately logged 18,049 anomalous AIS positions in the Gulf in its 23 October weekly overview. UKMTO said a small boat attached two explosive devices to a tanker's hull about 25 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Khasab on 29 October; the resulting engine-room fire was extinguished, the crew were safe, and the vessel continued to its next port of call, with no group claiming responsibility. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and army separately claimed, on the same day, that three tankers and then a fourth struck mines in and east of the strait (IRGC and army claims, unverified; no independent confirmation). The International Maritime Organization recorded at least 30 vessels hit in the Hormuz region in October through 27 October, injuring at least 16 seafarers — double September's 15 confirmed incidents and the worst month of the war, per CNBC's report of IMO data. Oman's Maritime Security Centre said its navy evacuated 25 crew members from the Panama-flagged tanker RITI after it was attacked and caught fire off Oman's coast on 30 October, with no casualties; UKMTO separately reported a tanker struck by an unknown projectile and set on fire about 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island the same day, crew safe (both confirmed, via AFP). Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on 30 October that three more tankers had "encountered incidents" on routes it considers unauthorized and were halted in the strait's southern waters, including a supertanker carrying about 2 million barrels that stopped after a mine explosion (IRGC claim, unverified; reporting on the tanker count was internally inconsistent and it is unclear whether these overlap with the 29 October claims). US Central Command's Adm. Brad Cooper said on 30 October that the strait's main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian mines and that Iran's navy had been destroyed; CENTCOM separately rejected an IRGC claim that Iran seized a US surveillance drone (CENTCOM claims, unverified). Kpler ship-tracking data put average Hormuz crude exports at about 11.1 mb/d for October through late in the month, about 2% below September, falling to 7.3 mb/d in the week to 28 October, more than 40% below the pre-war baseline, per CNBC. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on 30 October for a fresh round of talks; CBS reported signs of progress and said Iran was expected to respond to a revised Qatari proposal by the end of the week, while Axios said the sides remain divided over nuclear-site inspections and sanctions relief, and the Wall Street Journal reported Vice President Vance had separately written to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei on 28 October to try to restart talks. Axios and AP, citing diplomats, reported the US has also warned Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense military campaign after the 3 November midterms, corroborating earlier NYT reporting; officials said no final decision had been made. UKMTO reported a separate vessel struck by an unknown projectile in the strait on 1 November, relayed via a mayday call from a nearby merchant vessel; no casualties or claim of responsibility have been reported. Axios reported, citing sources, that Trump told Netanyahu by phone he wants to give Iran diplomacy more time before considering further strikes, after Secretary of State Rubio said on 31 October that no decision had been made on new strikes; Trump told reporters the US would end the war “one way or the other.” Brent and WTI each fell more than 3% on 2 November on the remarks, two days before the 3 November US midterm elections. A US official confirmed to Reuters on 3 November that US forces struck Iran's Qeshm Island, the strait's largest island, in what officials called a defensive response to Iran firing surface-to-air missiles at US assets; the Wall Street Journal reported the US has carried out periodic, unannounced "limited strikes" for several weeks to avoid signaling a return to major combat. A senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides remain far from a deal and Iran would respond forcefully to further US action. Brent and WTI both rebounded modestly on 3 November after Monday's steep selloff. On 2 November, US officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran's IRGC fired a surface-to-air missile at a US fighter jet near Qeshm Island, prompting the US aircraft to return fire in self-defense, and that US forces separately intercepted an IRGC missile launched from Qeshm Island that was targeting commercial shipping; ISW/CTP said it could not establish whether the launch was linked to earlier unconfirmed reports of US strikes near Jask (29 October) and Sirik (22 October). Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed on 3 November that three oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire after disabling their AIS and using an unauthorized route south of the strait (IRGC claim, unverified, per ISW/CTP); Iranian media cited the IRGC a day later saying four tankers had been destroyed in the same area and two more vessels detained, a toll that does not match the prior day's claim. UKMTO reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker's engine room on 3 November about 14 nautical miles northeast of Oman's Limah, with no casualties and no claim of responsibility. President Trump told Fox News the 3 November Qeshm Island strike hit an Iranian anti-aircraft facility, calling it a "minor attack" that "wasn't war," while Iranian state media reported Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had ordered the military to respond immediately to any threat. Mohsen Rezaei said on 3 November that the US reply to Iran's seven conditions for reopening the strait was "unconvincing" and that Washington must "fully and explicitly" address them before the strait reopens; Qatar's foreign ministry said both sides remain committed to the mediation process. Separately, Aramco CEO Amin Nasser told Reuters on 3 November the company is exploring additional export routes and overseas storage capacity, including a possible expansion of the 7 million b/d East-West Pipeline, and said more than 130 tanker attacks have been reported during the war with Gulf-to-Asia freight rates up more than 15-fold from a year earlier. UKMTO reported a tanker struck by two unidentified projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Qatar's Madinat ash-Shamal at 23:20 GMT on 4 November; it did not identify the vessel or flag, no group claimed responsibility, and UKMTO said most ships now decline to report attacks at all. The New York Times reported on 4 November, citing unnamed Pentagon officials, that thousands of US air and naval forces are positioned to resume major combat operations against Iran on Trump's order; Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said there should be "not the slightest inclination toward submission" to the US. Iran's Revolutionary Guards told Fars News on 5 November that a tanker hit a mine on an "illegal passageway" south of the strait and caught fire, and that a supertanker and the tugboat that approached to help also caught fire; Iran's army separately told IRNA that one tanker hit a mine early that day east of the strait and two more around midday, revising an earlier same-day count of three (IRGC and army claims, unverified; no independent confirmation). A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran has sent a new nuclear-program proposal to Washington via Qatari mediators, and the New York Times separately reported Iran is reviewing mediators' proposals; Qatar's foreign ministry said both sides remain committed to the process. Brent fell almost 9% on 4 November after the midterm result, rebounded 3.9% to a $98.29 settlement on 5 November (Bloomberg, via Rigzone), and eased slightly to about $98.19 on 6 November (Trading Economics); Rapidan Energy Group's Bob McNally told CNBC on 6 November he sees an 80% probability that military fighting resumes, citing the unresolved dispute over Iran's nuclear program. President Trump said on 6 November the US carried out a new, separate strike on an Iranian air-defense system on Qeshm Island — distinct from the 2 November strike there — calling it "minor" and saying it knocked the system out in "about 15 minutes, maybe five"; Iranian state media reported two explosions in Qeshm's Suza area, and no casualties were reported. Iraq's Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said on 8 November that Baghdad reached understandings with Washington to keep Iraqi crude moving through the strait via a shipping lane near Oman, putting Iraq's combined war and export losses at $60 billion; Reuters could not independently confirm the arrangement's terms. Separately on 8 November, Bloomberg reported that Trafigura, Vitol, Mercuria and ADNOC are seeking US Treasury licenses for about 50 of the roughly 1,600 US-sanctioned tankers, with no decisions finalized. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two tankers hit mines and caught fire on an "unauthorized route" on 7 November, and Fars News reported a third tanker also caught fire after an explosion (IRGC/Fars claims, unverified); separate blasts heard across southern Iran that evening, including on Qeshm Island, were not officially confirmed as missile strikes, and Iranian state television suggested they could be linked to Iran's own military activity rather than a US attack. UKMTO separately reported an incident involving a bulk carrier and military forces about 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan, UAE — the same day and area as the US military's disabling of a cargo vessel on 7 November, though it's unclear if they're the same incident. Brent eased further to about $96.9/bbl and TTF to about €86.9/MWh on 9 November (Trading Economics). A further wave of attacks hit Gulf and Hormuz shipping on 10-11 November: UKMTO and JMIC reported the tankers Fujairah Energy and NCC Fajr struck by unidentified projectiles, and the crude tanker Dominica Prosperity caught fire about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah's Mina Saqr port after a projectile hit its engine room, with all 22 crew evacuated safely (19 Indian nationals, per India's shipping minister); Reuters, citing MARISKS, named the operator as South Korea's Sinokor Maritime. JMIC's 12 November advisory tallied 181 maritime security incidents in the strait since 1 March. Brent rose back to about $95.4/bbl on 13 November (Trading Economics) as the renewed attacks offset recent de-escalation hopes. The IEA's Oil Market Report said Gulf crude exports excluding Oman reached about 15 million b/d in October (82% of pre-war levels), as UKMTO's latest weekly assessment counted 139 outbound and 169 inbound Hormuz transits, about 65% below pre-conflict levels, with eight maritime security incidents including seven tanker attacks. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards separately claimed a tanker carrying LNG struck a mine and exploded in the strait on 13 November, a day after claiming four oil tankers were hit by explosions (IRGC claims, unverified). Iran's navy said a further oil tanker caught fire on 14 November after hitting a naval mine in the eastern strait, per Iranian state media; Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report, and no vessel name or flag was given (IRGC/navy claim, unverified). Separately on 14 November, the Trump administration extended its Jones Act waiver allowing foreign-flagged vessels to carry oil, fuel, LNG and fertilizer between US ports for a further 90 days, citing high energy costs tied to the war. On 15 November UKMTO reported a tanker was attacked in the Arabian Gulf en route to the strait; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed two other tankers were struck and Iranian state media said five oil tankers had hit mines in the strait over the prior 48 hours (IRGC and state-media claims, unverified; Reuters found no independent confirmation). Iran's IRGC also launched drone strikes on a US early-warning radar in Bahrain on 13-14 November, which it called retaliation for an earlier US strike on a telecommunications tower in Hormozgan province; Bahrain's Defense Force said on 15 November it had intercepted the attack, the first such Iranian strike on a US-aligned base since September (IRGC claim, unverified; interception confirmed by Bahrain). A UKMTO advisory reported the Panama-flagged tanker On Phoenix was struck by an unknown projectile about three nautical miles off Oman while exiting the strait on 16 November, sparking an engine-room fire with the crew unharmed. ANZ analysts estimated Hormuz throughput at about 49% of pre-war levels even as Gulf exports keep recovering, Reuters reported on 17 November, as Brent eased to around $92.6/bbl. Iran's IRGC claimed a drone strike on a US radar system at Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain on 17 November; CENTCOM said the drones were intercepted with no damage to US equipment and no injuries (IRGC claim, unverified; interception confirmed by CENTCOM). The US then struck an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island the same day, a US military official said, describing it as a self-defense response (The National); Iran's Mehr news agency said the strikes caused no casualties or damage to infrastructure (Iranian claim, unverified). Brent fell further to about $92.0/bbl and WTI to $84.3/bbl by 18 November (Reuters) as rising US crude and gasoline stockpiles offset the renewed strikes. Iran's Artesh said its drones targeted Patriot air-defense systems at Kuwait's Ali al-Salem Air Base on 18 November; Kuwait's Army General Staff said its air defenses intercepted the drones, with no reported damage or casualties, and Bahrain's Defense Force said it repelled further Iranian aerial attacks the same day. Iran's IRGC Navy separately claimed a vessel struck a naval mine and exploded on an "unauthorized route" through the strait on 18 November, without naming the ship (IRGC claim, unverified); CTP-ISW said it has not observed evidence that Iran has successfully re-mined the strait's southern transit route. US Central Command's Joint Maritime Information Center said on 18 November it is expanding blockade enforcement to ship-to-ship transfers: a vessel receiving cargo at sea from a blockaded ship can now be treated as evading the blockade even if it never enters Iranian waters, and may be stopped, boarded, diverted or seized, with noncompliance risking disabling or destructive fire; neutral shipping to non-Iranian destinations is not targeted. The Lloyd's List Intelligence Strait of Hormuz Brief, published 19 November and covering October, said non-Iranian-linked transits rose to 550 for the month (up from 504 in September), the busiest since the war began, while UKMTO has recorded 163 confirmed incidents in the strait since the conflict started and seven attacks in the week to 11 November; CENTCOM separately said it has redirected 147 commercial vessels and disabled five since the blockade began. Iranian media (Fars News, IRGC-linked, and Tehran municipality outlet Hamshahri) reported on 18-20 November that Iran has loaded and crewed at least 14 tankers at Kharg Island to attempt a run through the blockade (Iranian claim, unverified); independent ship-tracking firm Windward separately counted at least 16 tankers anchored off Kharg as of 17 November and 31 already-laden sanctioned tankers waiting near the blockade line in the Arabian Sea, and tracking group UANI recorded a roughly 200,000-barrel ship-to-ship transfer between the tankers Olym and Hao Fan south of the island the same day, reported by Bloomberg (independent tracking, via The Maritime Executive and Euronews). CENTCOM reiterated that any vessel receiving cargo from a blockaded ship is also treated as evading it; TankerTrackers.com, which first flagged the Kharg staging, later said a full convoy breakout was "wishful thinking." Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the blockade "must be broken" and Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi called it "an act of war," while Iranian officials warned of a "fierce military response," including strikes on energy infrastructure across the Gulf, if the convoy is intercepted (Iranian claims, unverified). On 21 November Iran launched two waves of drone and missile attacks on US-linked bases in Bahrain, including Sheikh Isa Air Base; Bahrain's government confirmed the attacks and said its air defenses intercepted them, with a fire reported at a nearby civilian industrial compound; Bahrain's Interior Ministry said the attack injured two people, per CTP-ISW's 23 November Iran Update, correcting this entry's earlier report of no injuries (confirmed, via Bahrain's government). The IRGC's unverified claim to have hit Patriot air-defense batteries and a radar system was not confirmed by Bahrain or the US. UKMTO reported two further tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in or near the strait the same day, and Iran's navy separately claimed a tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire (IRGC claim, unverified). Qatari mediators held further talks with Iranian officials on 20-21 November; Araghchi said reopening the strait remains possible if the US ends the blockade, lifts sanctions and acknowledges "past mistakes." Brent rose to about $92.57/bbl on 20 November (Trading Economics), up slightly from $91.98 the day before, as the renewed attacks offset bearish US inventory data. UKMTO data reported by Al Jazeera on 22 November showed Hormuz transits fell 15% week-on-week to 263 ships in the week of 12-18 November, with oil tankers down to 37 from 52 the week before; before the war about 135 ships a day passed through the strait. The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026, released 19 November, put cumulative Gulf oil export losses from the disruption at about 2.8 billion barrels since the war began. Brent crude settled down 3.5% at $89.37/bbl on 23 November as traders unwound hedges against a feared weekend US escalation against Iran after Trump signaled more time for diplomacy (Rigzone, via Reuters pricing); Kpler data cited by Gulf News put Hormuz-specific flows at about 10 million b/d by 10 November, down from 13.4 million at the start of the month. Brent rebounded 2.3% to a $91.40 settlement on 24 November as the prior day's selloff partly reversed (Bloomberg, via Rigzone); MarineTraffic data cited by Al Jazeera the same day showed vessels entering and exiting the Gulf fell to 125 in the week of 17-23 November from 226 in the week of 1-7 November, a roughly 40% drop. Iran's navy and IRGC separately claimed on 24 November that tankers struck mines and caught fire east of the strait in a zone it calls restricted, with army chief Amir Hatami and IRGC navy chief Ali Ozmaei saying Iran is tightening control of the strait (IRGC/navy claims, unverified, per Tasnim News Agency; no independent confirmation found). Brent jumped 3.5% to a $94.61 settlement and WTI rose 2% to $83.68 on 25 November after Yemen's Houthis said they struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery and export terminal with a missile; Critical Threats Project/ISW reviewed satellite imagery showing smoke plumes near the site and assessed it as likely confirming a strike (Houthi claim, unverified, with independent satellite-imagery corroboration per ISW/CTP; Saudi authorities made no public confirmation). Saudi Joint Forces Command spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki separately confirmed Jizan port was hit by a projectile the same day, causing minor damage; the Houthis also claimed a strike on Jeddah port, which Saudi authorities did not confirm.

bab-el-mandeb.summary: The Houthis have enforced a 'ban' on Saudi-linked shipping since 20 July, hitting ships (Tihamah 12 Aug, Bahri VLCC off Yanbu 24 Aug) and seizing Mocha and Red Sea islands on 10-11 Sep. Tanker transits fell sharply; overall transits were ~15% below pre-ban levels by late August. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive ('Operation Yemen Dawn') around 3-5 Oct, backed by a reported 100 Saudi-led coalition jets, and said they had taken full control of the strait plus Dhubab town, its airport and the road to Mokha; on 9 Oct the Saudi-led coalition said it struck 136 further 'high-value' Houthi targets and Yemeni officials additionally claimed Mayyun (Perim) Island, which the Houthis had seized in September, had been retaken. On 10 Oct Houthi media said they repelled the Yemeni-government push on Mayyun and still hold the island, directly contradicting the 9 Oct claim. A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend of 10-11 Oct killed at least 13 people, the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade, and the Saudi-led coalition responded on 13 Oct with strikes on Houthi-linked sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar, including a Yemen Petroleum Company fuel depot the company said held no stocks; Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree threatened retaliation against Aramco's Dhahran headquarters and a Saudi refinery. Both sides' claims about territorial and shipping-lane control remain unverified and independent confirmation is unavailable, so the status here is unchanged. JMIC recorded 58 transits through Bab el-Mandeb over 22-24 October, against a baseline near 61/day, continuing the sharp falloff from normal traffic. A JMIC advisory distributed by UKMTO (dated 5 Nov) showed transits recovering modestly even as the security picture stayed volatile: an industry tracker counted an average of about 34 commercial transits a day from 1-4 November (daily counts 38, 37, 35 and 26), up from about 28/day the prior week but still below pre-ban levels; JMIC logged one unconfirmed suspicious-activity report in the southern Red Sea (ref. MSCIO 168/26) and said the strait remains open to commercial shipping. Yemeni government-aligned Southern Armed Forces announced on 15 November they had withdrawn from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area to reinforce Aden; other factions, including the Southern Giants Brigades, also pulled back to positions in Lahij governorate. ISW/CTP assessed the withdrawal was a likely response to a Houthi offensive in southeastern Lahij on 12 November that threatened the Mokha-Aden supply route. The pullback let the Houthis reoccupy the Ras Menhali peninsula and Perim (Mayyun) Island, which overlook the strait's southern approach, according to satellite-imagery analysis reported by The Maritime Executive — reversing the Yemeni government's early-October claim to have retaken the island during 'Operation Yemen Dawn.' Commercial shipping through the strait has continued without a reported rise in attacks since the handover. CTP-ISW assessed on 17 November that the Houthis' gains since 15 November could make it easier for the group to target international shipping, and that war-risk insurance rates are unlikely to return to pre-crisis levels for a long time after the crisis ends.

suez-canal.summary: Container traffic has recovered further: Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 1,228 September transits (106.3 million dwt), up 21% year on year but still 39% below pre-crisis levels, and called it the busiest month since December 2023. BIMCO/Clarksons put average weekly container-ship capacity through the canal at 753,000 TEU in the first two weeks of October — just over half of 2023's 1.46 million TEU and, BIMCO said, the first time since the Houthi campaign began that transits topped 50% of pre-disruption levels; the canal carried 36% of container capacity routed via Suez or the Cape of Good Hope, up from an 8% average over 2024-mid 2026 but still below the roughly 80% share before the attacks. Most tankers using the canal in September were carrying Russian crude to India. Carriers are starting to shift some Asia-Europe strings back to Suez: Hapag-Lloyd and Gemini alliance partner Maersk now route five Far East-South Europe services, one Far East-North Europe service and two India-Europe connections via the canal rather than the Cape of Good Hope, including the ME1/IOS India-Europe string switched over on 2 Nov (first westbound sailing from Salalah 4 Nov, first eastbound from Tangier around 12-13 Nov); other northern European services still sail via the Cape and further shifts depend on Red Sea security.

east-west-pipeline.summary: Shut 11 Sep after drone strikes on pumping stations (launched from Iraq); restarted around 21-22 Sep. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on 6 Oct that flow had reached 5.8 million bpd — about 83% of its 7 mb/d capacity — with roughly 4 mb/d of that rerouted to Yanbu on the Red Sea to bypass Hormuz, about 4% of global oil supply. Flows were as low as ~2 mb/d in August (Kpler) after Houthi attacks on the Red Sea route. Aramco is also in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on this bypass system. The Houthis said on 26 Oct they struck the pipeline's pumping stations again; Aramco and Saudi authorities have not confirmed any damage or flow impact (unverified: Houthi claim). Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said on 9 November the pipeline was hit in the Medina region, causing a brief fire that was extinguished with no injuries and no effect on operations, per the Saudi Press Agency; no party was identified. The Houthis said on 12 November they struck a pumping station on the pipeline and an oil facility at Yanbu, and made a similar claim on 15 November against two more pumping stations; Saudi Arabia did not respond to either claim, and Reuters and CTP-ISW both said they could not verify them (Houthi claims, unverified).

yanbu-terminal.summary: Saudi Arabia's main Hormuz-bypass outlet remains under Houthi missile and drone threat and subject to a declared Houthi ban on Saudi-linked shipping. Throughput has recovered with the East-West pipeline: the energy minister said on 6 Oct that pipeline flow reached 5.8 million bpd (83% of capacity), with about 4 million bpd rerouted here to bypass Hormuz. Aramco is in talks to formalize long-term shuttle contracts built on this route. France is sending air defences. On 19 October the Houthis separately claimed a strike on an Aramco facility at Yanbu itself, with no independent or Saudi confirmation. Saudi-led coalition air defenses intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the Yanbu area, along with one toward Taif, on 24 October; no damage to Aramco facilities was reported.

ras-laffan-lng.summary: Two of 14 LNG trains and a GTL plant were destroyed on 19 Mar (12.8 mtpa, ~17% of capacity, 3-5 years to repair); the remaining trains provide about 83% of operational capacity, with 3-4 kept running at low rates for a faster restart. Exports depend on Hormuz: QatarEnergy restarted shipments in September using older 'mother' tankers that sail loaded, often dark, and transfer cargo to 'daughter' vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman, with Qatar recalling leased-out ships, chartering outside tonnage at roughly 10x normal freight and recruiting Indonesian crews at double-to-triple pay. Deliveries reached about a third of prewar levels by late September — April-September exports were down almost 90% year on year — at an estimated cost to Qatar of roughly $1bn a week (Bloomberg); the IMF estimates Qatar's economy could contract 15.6% this year. On 19 October a Qatari LNG cargo loaded in August sailed through the Red Sea, with ship-tracking data suggesting it was headed to Poland (Bloomberg) — a route most vessels have avoided since 2023 — while UKMTO reported a skiff fired on an LNG tanker in the Gulf of Aden near Al Mukalla the same day; the vessel's security team returned fire and it continued its voyage. Bloomberg reported Nov 10, citing Kpler and Copernicus ship-tracking data, that loadings have since risen to a 10-day moving average of 13-15 cargoes so far in November — roughly half the pre-war pace, up from about 11 in October — with 11 laden tankers exiting the Strait of Hormuz in the 10 days through Nov 8. Poland's Orlen said Nov 11 it had terminated one of its long-term LNG contracts with QatarEnergy (running to 2034, worth about €570m this year) over the delivery disruption, the first such cancellation by a QatarEnergy customer; Orlen keeps a second supply contract with Qatar.

kharg-island.summary: The terminal was intact after US strikes on military targets (14 Mar). Iranian exports have been under a US naval blockade since 14 July, and the US struck an Iranian tanker off Kharg on 5 Sep. Tracking group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), corroborated by Bloomberg vessel-tracking, reported at least 50 Iranian tankers backed up along Iran's coast as of early October, 11 of them laden and anchored east of Kharg with none loading there on 5 Oct; Iran loaded no crude at all in September — the first such month since the war began, per Kpler — with exports falling from about 966,000 b/d in July to roughly 50,000 b/d, as no Iranian crude is known to have crossed the blockade line since 14 July. Reuters reported on 16 October, citing UANI tracking and SynMax satellite analysis, that Iran has nonetheless moved at least 4.1 million barrels of LPG on eight tankers out of the Gulf of Oman since mid-July (some transferred near Shinas and Sohar, Oman, before onward shipment via Malaysia, likely to China) and one jet-fuel cargo that reached Myanmar in September; six of those nine tankers are under US sanctions. CENTCOM said the blockade is 'ironclad,' reporting four vessels disabled and 135 turned back over three months; a US Treasury spokesperson cautioned the shipping data 'should be taken with a grain of salt' since vessels can spoof location or identity. Bloomberg reported on 19 October that no tankers have docked at Kharg's crude-loading terminals since late August — the longest idle stretch since the war began — and that UKMTO logged 25 ships targeted in and around the strait in the first two weeks of October, up from 18 in September and 15 in August. The Wall Street Journal reported on 21 October, citing Kpler tracking, that Iran's floating oil stockpile beyond the US blockade line has fallen from about 90 million barrels in mid-July to roughly 29 million, as no new Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since mid-July and little remains to draw down; Kpler estimated the stockpile could be exhausted around mid-October at the recent drawdown pace, mostly to China. US Central Command's Joint Maritime Information Center said on 18 November it is expanding blockade enforcement to ship-to-ship transfers, so a vessel receiving cargo at sea from a blockaded ship can be treated as evading the blockade even without entering Iranian waters — closing off a transfer route trackers say Iran has used to move cargo past the blockade line.

ras-tanura-terminal.summary: Loadings are constrained by the Hormuz situation but have partly offset the Yanbu/East-West pipeline outage: Aramco has sold ~60 million barrels of Ras Tanura crude for ship-to-ship transfer at Sohar, Oman this month and next, shipped out via Hormuz by shuttle tanker. Yemen's Houthis said on 25 Nov they struck the refinery and export terminal complex with a missile; ISW/CTP reviewed satellite imagery showing smoke plumes and assessed it as likely confirming a hit (Houthi claim, unverified, with independent satellite-imagery corroboration). Saudi Aramco made no public statement on the claim, and no report found so far shows an effect on loadings.

fujairah.summary: The UAE's main outlet outside Hormuz, fed by the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline (~1.5 mb/d), has been attacked repeatedly (14 and 16 Mar, 4 May). Kpler data showed exports rising to 1.62 mb/d in March from 1.17 mb/d in February as volumes were rerouted there. Fujairah also underpins the shuttle-tanker system that lets Gulf crude bypass the Strait of Hormuz, with VLCCs waiting offshore there while shuttle tankers make the riskier transit to load and transfer cargo. Tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg showed at least 10 VLCCs and several Suezmax tankers approaching Fujairah had stopped or reversed course in the days before 13 Oct amid near-daily attacks around the strait, raising the risk of slower bypass flows at a time of an already acute global tanker shortage.

shah-gas-field.summary: Shut after a drone attack caused a fire on Mar 16 (Reuters). Production was increasing again by early May (MEES), and partner Occidental said on May 6 that constraints there should ease by the end of June, then on Aug 6 that it expected normal international volumes in the third quarter. Whether the plant is back at full rates has not been reported, so it may now be running normally. Status after August not verified.

basra-oil-terminal.summary: Iraq halted its southern terminals around Mar 12 after two tankers were attacked off Basra (Argus), and loadings resumed on Apr 17 (Reuters). Exports recovered from about 0.1 mb/d in May to about 2 mb/d in August, about 2.65 mb/d in September and about 3.5 mb/d in October — close to the 3.3–3.5 mb/d pre-war level — after Iraq said it reached understandings with Washington on 8 November to keep exports moving through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman (Reuters, citing Iraqi energy officials and Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein). No damage to the terminal has been reported.

primorsk-terminal.summary: Drone strikes on Mar 22–23 set storage tanks on fire and stopped loadings until Mar 26. Satellite images showed at least eight tanks damaged, at least 40% of the port's storage (Reuters). It is loading: crude shipments were just over 1.1 mb/d in the first half of May (Reuters, LSEG data), with fuel loadings below capacity. Repair of the tanks has not been reported. Status after May not verified.

ust-luga-terminal.summary: Strikes in late March damaged eight product tanks, about a quarter of storage, and some berths, and oil loadings stopped from Mar 25 until Apr 4 (Reuters). Loadings were about 0.6 mb/d in the first half of May (Reuters). On Aug 14 Novatek's gas condensate complex at the port was damaged (Reuters, industry sources). Loading status after May not verified.

moscow-refinery.summary: Stopped processing crude after a drone attack on Sep 20 set both primary distillation units on fire; repairs could take several weeks (Reuters, three industry sources). It had been knocked out by strikes on Jun 16 and 18 and restarted before being hit again. A Reuters list of Oct 7 still shows it halted; no restart has been reported.
